title: Slab-bucket batching latency exploration
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an exploratory test series that tries a slab/bucket-based batching approach as an alternative to the current age/size/time heuristics. The core idea: partition incoming requests into small number of "slabs" by a cheap, online affinity (e.g., estimated token-length band or KV-cache-affinity tag) and run per-slab timers and size thresholds to control coalescing. Goal is to reduce long-tail latency for heterogeneous request mixes while keeping overall throughput high and wasted compute low.

Problem context and motivation:
- Current continuous-batching controller groups by arrival time with a single global timeout and max-batch-size. Works well for homogeneous traffic but struggles when a small fraction of large/slow requests (long sequences or heavy decode cost) back up and cause head-of-line blocking for short fast requests.
- We've tried priority demotion and age-weighted batching (see other notes) but still observe p99.9 spikes under mixed workloads, especially when skews in sequence length correlate with bursts.
- Slab/bucket idea: keep lanes that aim to be more homogeneous in service time so that small/fast requests don't wait behind large ones. Slabs are soft: a request is mapped to a slab, but admission/fallback can cross slabs to avoid wasted GPU cycles if a slab idles.

Hypotheses:
1) Per-slab timeouts tuned to slab-specific size distributions will reduce p99/p999 for short-request slabs without hurting overall throughput.
2) Slab-level batching reduces KV-cache thrash because requests with similar prefix lengths and recent KV usage are grouped, increasing cache hit locality.
3) Too many slabs increase scheduling overhead and reduce batching efficiency - there's a sweet spot at 3-6 slabs for our production mix.

Mapping function candidates (cheap to compute at ingress):
- Token-length band: [<=32], [33-128], [129-512], [>512] (fast to estimate from prompt metadata)
- KV-affinity tag: hashed recent conversation id or user id % N
- Model-variant grouping: quantized by decode config (top-k vs nucleus)
We tested token-length band + small heuristic that puts very-short requests into the "express" slab.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
Variables:
- Num slabs: 2, 3, 4, 6
- Per-slab timeout (ms): tuned per slab in {10, 20, 50, 80, 150}
- Global max_batch_size: 8, 16, 32
- Admission demotion threshold: allow cross-slab fill when slab idle for > X ms (X in {5, 15, 50})
- Backfill policy: strict vs soft cross-slab (soft allows partial fill from other slabs while preserving one slot for own slab)

Workloads:
- Baseline homogeneous short: 90% <=32 tokens, 10% 100 tokens (poisson arrivals at 1k rps)
- Mixed: 60% <=32, 30% 128-256, 10% >512 (bursty arrivals with microbursts every 10s)
- Heavy-long tail: 30% short, 50% mid, 20% long (>512 tokens)

Observability and measurement:
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 latency, GPU token throughput, GPU utilization, batch fill distribution, tokens per second, tokens per GPU-second cost estimate, KV-cache hit ratio (approx), percent of cross-slab fills.
- Traces: sampled request traces (Jaeger) instrumented with slab id, batch id, batch size, flush cause (timeout/size/preemption), queue_time, exec_time, total_latency.
- Profiling: pprof on runner threads, flamegraphs of batch-assembly hot paths, small eBPF hist for syscalls during device copies.

Key results (high level):
- Best tradeoff point for mixed workload: num_slabs=3, per-slab timeouts = {express:10ms, mid:30ms, long:80ms}, max_batch_size=16, backfill soft with X=15ms. This reduced p99.9 for short requests from ~950ms to ~220ms in our synthetic mixed trace while keeping throughput within 6% of baseline.
- GPU utilization: roughly flat (within +-4%) across best slab configs vs baseline because cross-slab soft backfill kept GPUs busy.
- Batch size distribution: express slab had avg batch size 6, mid slab 10, long slab 12; we observed lower variance in exec_time per slab compared to global batching.
- KV-cache affinity: measured a small improvement in cache-local hits (from 72% to 79%) for mid slab; likely because similar-length requests tend to have similar prefix patterns in our dataset.
- Overhead: scheduling CPU cost increased by ~8%-12% depending on number of slabs (more slabs -> more bookkeeping). At 6 slabs overhead was noticeable and started to hurt throughput at high rps.
- Backfill behavior: strict backfill preserved predictability for express slab but underutilized GPU during some bursts; soft backfill was better overall.

Representative trace snippets (anonymized):
- Before (global): short request arrived at t=1000.3ms, joined batch with one long request, queue time 180ms, exec 22ms, total 202ms, p99.9 sample = 920ms (due to long request preceding decode).
- After (slab): same short request mapped to express slab, queue time 9ms (waited for express timeout), exec 2.8ms, total 11.8ms.

Failure modes observed and mitigations:
- Low fan-in slabs starve fill: if a slab has few arrivals, small batches can hurt throughput. Mitigation: allow soft cross-slab fills after short grace period (15ms) and maintain a minimum reserved slot policy so express slab isn't fully consumed by backfill.
- Misclassification at ingress puts long requests into express slab (bad heuristics). Mitigation: simple length check accepted; but also add a second-pass at batch-assembly that demotes a request if its estimated cost > slab median.
- Increased CPU scheduling overhead on high concurrency hosts. Mitigation: move simple mapping and per-slab queue operations into a low-contention ring buffer and avoid locks in hot path. Consider eBPF for ingress classification if CPU becomes the limiter.

Operational suggestions and rollout plan:
1) Nightly canary: deploy slab-batching as opt-in config flag on dedicated cluster with 10% traffic, instrument p50/p95/p99/p99.9 and cross-check costs.
2) Start with 3 slabs (express/mid/long) and soft backfill policy. Monitor CPU scheduling overhead and set alerts if scheduling CPU exceeds baseline +15%.
3) Add a small ML-based estimator later for per-request decode cost if heuristics show persistent misclassification in production.
4) Add observability card in console: per-slab latency heatmap, per-slab batch fill histogram, cross-slab fill rate, and slab misclassification counter.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Adaptive slab reconfiguration: can we dynamically merge/split slabs based on sliding-window statistics to keep overhead low while adapting to traffic shifts? Prototype idea: every 30s compute slab entropy and consider merge if two adjacent slabs have similar latency distributions.
- Interaction with KV cache eviction and prefix caching: does slab grouping amplify beneficial cache locality across models? Needs longer-run tests with real customer traffic.
- Canary failure modes: how does slab fallback work with model rollouts (pinning, canary)? Need to ensure slab metadata passes through rollout machinery to avoid unexpected cache/pinning mismatches.

Action items (owners):
- Diego: implement soft backfill prototype in the batch-assembly code path (PR referenced above). Target: 2 weeks.
- Priya: add slab observability panels to the console (heatmaps + histograms). Target: 1 week.
- Ethan: run 48h mixed-signal canary on dedicated cluster and produce consolidated metrics. Target: 10 days.
- Ava: write follow-up note on dynamic slab merging and quantify expected CPU cost savings. Target: 2 weeks.

Appendix: quick commands and traces used
- Local replay harness: ./tools/replay --trace mixed-202402 --rps 1200 --slab-config 3 --timeout-params express=10,mid=30,long=80 --backfill soft --max-batch 16
- Sample pprof invocation on runner: go tool pprof http://runner-host:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
- Jaeger link (sample): (redacted) span tags: {slab_id:express, batch_fill:6, flush:timeout}

Notes: This is exploratory. Results are promising but not final—tuning knobs interact. The slab approach looks like a useful lever to reduce tail latency for short requests without large throughput regressions, but it requires careful backfill policy and modest CPU investment.

If reviewers want raw CSV results from the 48 permutations we ran, I can export and drop into the same directory.
